title: 158. Quantitative Relationships & Measurement: Interpreting Logarithmic Scales in Claims
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Equal Intervals on a Base-10 Logarithmic Scale
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the meaning of equal intervals on a base-10 logarithmic axis.
questions.question: On a base-\(10\) logarithmic axis, two points are \(1\) unit apart. What does this indicate about the actual values?

options.label: A
options.text: The actual values have a ratio of \(10\) to \(1\).

questions.explanation: On a base-\(10\) logarithmic scale, equal intervals represent equal multiplicative factors. A difference of \(1\) log unit means \(\log_{10}(x_2)-\log_{10}(x_1)=1\), so \(\frac{x_2}{x_1}=10^1=10\). Thus the values have a \(10\)-to-\(1\) ratio, not a difference of \(1\).
questions.hint: Write the distance of \(1\) unit as a difference of two base-\(10\) logarithms, then rewrite it as a statement about the two actual values.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the amplitude ratio from a difference in Richter magnitudes.
questions.question: On the Richter scale, each whole-number increase represents about \(10\) times greater ground-motion amplitude. How many times greater is the amplitude of a magnitude \(6\) earthquake than a magnitude \(4\) earthquake?
questions.explanation: The difference in magnitude is \(6-4=2\). Each unit corresponds to a factor of \(10\), so the ratio is \(10^2=100\). Therefore the magnitude \(6\) earthquake has about \(100\) times greater amplitude.
questions.hint: Use the magnitude difference as the exponent of \(10\).

questions.learningObjective: Determine the intensity ratio from a difference in decibels.
questions.question: A sound increases by \(20\text{ dB}\). On the decibel scale, an increase of \(10\text{ dB}\) corresponds to \(10\) times greater intensity. How many times greater is the intensity after the increase?
questions.explanation: An increase of \(20\text{ dB}\) is two \(10\text{-dB}\) steps. Each \(10\text{-dB}\) step multiplies intensity by \(10\), so the total factor is \(10\times 10=100\). Therefore the intensity is \(100\) times greater.
questions.hint: Count how many \(10\text{-dB}\) steps are in \(20\text{ dB}\) and multiply by \(10\) for each step.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a logarithmic scale is used for data spanning many orders of magnitude.
questions.question: A graph uses a logarithmic vertical axis to display values from \(1\) to \(1{,}000{,}000\). What is the main reason for using this scale?

options.label: A
options.text: It makes every numerical difference appear the same size.

options.label: B
options.text: It compresses a very large range while preserving multiplicative relationships.

questions.explanation: A logarithmic scale compresses a wide range of values into a smaller visual space. Equal visual intervals correspond to equal multiplicative factors, so ratios and orders of magnitude remain visible. It does not make all absolute differences equal.
questions.hint: Think about how a log scale treats multiplication and large ranges.

questions.concept: Straight Line on a Logarithmic Axis
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a straight-line trend on a logarithmic vertical axis.
questions.question: A graph with a logarithmic vertical axis shows a straight line rising steadily over time. What does this imply about the actual values?

options.label: A
options.text: They increase by equal amounts each period.

options.label: B
options.text: They increase by equal multiplicative factors each period.

questions.explanation: On a logarithmic axis, equal vertical changes represent equal ratios. A straight rising line therefore means the actual values are multiplied by the same factor in each time period, which is exponential growth, not constant addition.
questions.hint: A straight line means the same vertical step in every period. Ask what kind of change in the actual value produces the same step on a logarithmic axis.

questions.concept: Log Difference for a Doubling Claim
questions.learningObjective: Estimate the logarithmic difference corresponding to a doubling claim.
questions.question: A claim states that Value \(A\) is twice Value \(B\). On a base-\(10\) logarithmic axis, what is the approximate difference in log units?
questions.explanation: If \(A=2B\), then the ratio is \(2\). The base-\(10\) log difference is \(\log_{10}(2)\approx 0.301\). So the claim corresponds to a difference of about \(0.30\) log units, not \(2\) log units.
questions.hint: On a base-\(10\) log axis, the distance between two values equals the logarithm of their ratio.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate an intensity ratio from a larger decibel difference.
questions.question: A sound's intensity level increases by \(30\text{ dB}\). How many times greater is the new intensity compared with the original intensity?
questions.explanation: A \(10\text{-dB}\) increase means \(10\) times greater intensity. A \(30\text{-dB}\) increase is three \(10\text{-dB}\) steps, so the factor is \(10^3=1000\). Therefore the intensity is \(1000\) times greater.
questions.hint: Convert the decibel increase into a power of \(10\).

questions.concept: Interpreting a One-Unit Difference on a Log Axis
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a claim that compares two values using a logarithmic axis.
questions.question: A claim says, "Country X's cases are \(10\) times Country Y's cases because the X bar is one log unit higher." Under what condition is this claim valid?

options.label: A
options.text: It is never valid because logarithmic axes cannot compare counts.

options.label: B
options.text: It is valid if the axis is base-\(10\) logarithmic, because one unit higher means a \(10\)-times ratio.

questions.explanation: On a base-\(10\) logarithmic scale, a difference of \(1\) unit means the ratio of the actual values is \(10^1=10\). Therefore the claim is valid if the axis is base-\(10\) logarithmic. Logarithmic axes can compare counts when interpreted correctly.
questions.hint: Check whether the axis is base-\(10\) logarithmic and what a one-unit difference represents.

questions.concept: Three-Unit Difference on a Base-10 Log Axis
questions.learningObjective: Determine the actual ratio from a three-unit difference on a base-10 log axis.
questions.question: On a base-\(10\) logarithmic axis, two values differ by \(3\) units. What is the ratio of the larger value to the smaller value?
questions.explanation: A difference of \(3\) log units means the ratio is \(10^3=1000\). Thus the larger value is \(1000\) times the smaller value, not \(3\) times.
questions.hint: Raise \(10\) to the power equal to the number of log units.

questions.concept: Misreading Additive Change on a Log Scale
questions.learningObjective: Identify the error in treating a log-scale increase as an additive increase.
questions.question: A claim says, "The line rose by \(2\) units on the base-\(10\) log scale, so the actual value increased by \(2\)." What is wrong with this claim?

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing is wrong; logarithmic scales preserve additive differences.

options.label: B
options.text: On a base-\(10\) log scale, a \(2\)-unit increase means the actual value is multiplied by \(10^2=100\), not increased by \(2\).

questions.explanation: A logarithmic scale converts multiplicative changes into additive changes in the log value. A rise of \(2\) units on a base-\(10\) log scale means \(\log_{10}(x_2)-\log_{10}(x_1)=2\), so \(\frac{x_2}{x_1}=10^2=100\). The actual value is multiplied by \(100\), not increased by \(2\).
questions.hint: Write the rise as \(\log_{10}(x_2)-\log_{10}(x_1)=2\) and work out how \(x_2\) is related to \(x_1\).
